newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Gutnick disappointed with RBA gold sale.
newsitem.headline: Gutnick disappointed with RBA gold sale.

text.p: Australian mining entrepreneur Joseph Gutnick said on Friday he was disappointed by the Reserve Bank of Australia's sell-down of 167-tonnes of gold but did not see the move creating problems for forward selling.
"I do not think (hedging) will be affected by the Reserve Bank, I am not aware of that problem," Gutnick, chairman and managing director of Great Central Mines, told Reuters.
He added that his company had sold forward more than two million ounces of gold.
Under forward selling, mines borrow gold from central banks or, less usually, commercial banks to sell before they have mined the equivalent amount as defence against falling prices.
One senior London-based gold dealer said the RBA sale would make Australian gold miners' aggressive forward selling policy more difficult to complete, forcing them to look elsewhere to borrow.
"I cannot see that as being a problem," Gutnick said.
"You can hedge in London or COMEX, there is no restriction on hedging," he said.
Gutnick said he found the RBA's decision to sell down its reserves "very disappointing and astonishingly surprising" when Australia was such a major producer of gold.
"They should be supporting the gold industry by showing confidence in the price of gold," he said.
Gutnick said the impact of the move, news of which saw gold prices slump to a 12-year low in late New York trade, would be a "short-term aberration".
"I do not believe that one or two or three central banks can change the intrinsic value that exists for gold," he said.

"There is very strong demand in Asia and the fact that there has been that much selling and it has been absorbed is a very positive sign," he said, adding it was no wonder the gold price had been "sloppy" with the Australian central bank's sales.

Asked about the impact on the share prices of Australian gold producers, Gutnick said in the short-term it would "take away some of the confidence" and may attract corporate plays from overseas gold producers and investors.

"(News of the sales) was not a good thing to wake up to, not because it will in any way affect the profitability of the miners in AustralIa, just the lack of confidence in the gold industry which was disappointing to see from the Australian government," he said.
Gutnick is chairman or chief executive of nine public companies, led by GCM and Centaur Mining and Exploration Ltd.
At 1.10 p.m. (0310 GMT), Great Central was trading at A$2.42, down 10 cents on Thursday's close. Centaur was at A$1.60, nine cents off against a slightly firmer overall market.
